content: 1. Chapter 3 provides a detailed description of the research gaps identified in relation to the recommendations. Chapter 4 elaborates on these gaps. Additionally, annexes are included to provide background information for the recommendations in Chapter 2, including evaluations of the evidence supporting key recommendations. 2. This guidance will undergo a review in 2016. A guideline review group will be convened to assess new evidence and revise the recommendations if necessary. 3. The Department of Pandemic and Epidemic Diseases at the WHO headquarters in Geneva, in collaboration with its internal partners, will oversee the coordination of the guideline update. This process will adhere to the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. 4. If new evidence emerges that necessitates changes to the current recommendations, the guideline will be updated prior to the scheduled review date. 5. Updated summary guidance documents and training materials specifically designed for healthcare workers are currently being prepared as companion resources to this document. 6. Recommendations include the placement of patients infected or colonized with the same laboratory-identified pathogens in the same designated unit, zone, or ward to reduce transmission risks. Similarly, patients with the same suspected diagnosis, based on epidemiological and clinical information, should be grouped together to minimize the spread of acute respiratory infection (ARI) pathogens to healthcare workers and other patients. 7. The use of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) should be determined by risk assessment, considering the procedure and suspected pathogen. For patients presenting with ARI syndromes, PPE may include medical masks (surgical or procedural), gloves, long-sleeved gowns, and eye protection (goggles or face shields). 8. During aerosol-generating procedures associated with an increased risk of ARI pathogen transmission, healthcare workers should use PPE, including gloves, long-sleeved gowns, eye protection, and facial masks (surgical, procedural, or particulate respirators). Examples of such procedures include cardiopulmonary resuscitation and bronchoscopy. 9. Aerosol-generating procedures should ideally be performed in adequately ventilated single rooms to reduce the risk of ARI transmission. 10. Healthcare workers caring for patients at high risk of severe or complicated influenza disease should be vaccinated to reduce illness and mortality among these patients. 11. The use of ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) for air disinfection is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. 12. Additional infection prevention and control (IPC) precautions should be implemented at the time of patient admission and continued throughout the duration of symptomatic illness. These precautions should be modified based on the pathogen and patient information. Standard precautions should always be followed. 13. There is no evidence to support the routine use of laboratory tests to determine the duration of IPC precautions. 14. Acute respiratory infections (ARIs) are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality from infectious diseases worldwide, with nearly four million deaths annually. The majority of these deaths (98%) are due to lower respiratory tract infections, particularly in infants, children, and the elderly, and predominantly in lowand middle-income countries. 15. ARIs are a frequent cause of healthcare consultations and admissions, especially in pediatric services. Bacteria, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae, are a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections, but viruses or mixed viral-bacterial infections are the most common pathogens causing ARIs. 16. ARIs with epidemic or pandemic potential pose significant public health risks and require special precautions and preparedness measures. 17. This document provides recommendations and information on IPC measures for ARIs in healthcare settings, with a focus on ARIs that have the potential for rapid spread and may cause epidemics or pandemics. These guidelines address ARIs that cause severe disease in individuals with normal immune systems and may constitute a public health emergency of international concern. 18. Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) is caused by the SARS coronavirus (SARS-CoV), which can infect both animals and humans. The disease was first reported in Asia in February 2003 and spread to over 24 countries before the outbreak was contained. While SARS is not currently circulating among humans, it may still be present in animal hosts and could re-emerge. 19. Human-to-human transmission of SARS occurs primarily through droplets or direct contact, though short-range transmission via infectious respiratory aerosols of various sizes may also occur. 20. Influenza viruses can infect multiple species, including humans, birds, pigs, horses, and seals. Birds are the primary reservoir for influenza A viruses. Seasonal influenza epidemics are caused by viruses well-adapted to human hosts, while new influenza viruses emerging from other species may cause pandemics. 21. Direct transmission of avian influenza viruses, such as H5N1, H7N9, and others, to humans has been documented and often results in high fatality rates. However, efficient or sustained human-to-human transmission of avian influenza A (H5N1) has not been demonstrated. 22. The 2009 pandemic influenza A (H1N1) virus resulted from genetic reassortment of swine, avian, and human viruses and spread efficiently through human-to-human transmission, causing a global pandemic. 23. Novel ARIs with high public health impact continue to emerge, often originating from animal reservoirs. Examples include human cases of influenza A (H7N9) in 2013 and Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) coronavirus in 2012. 24. Factors contributing to the emergence and spread of infectious diseases include changes in human demographics and behavior, new technologies, economic development, increased international travel, microbial adaptation, poor public health measures, and close contact with domestic or wild animals. 25. When a new infectious disease is identified, its modes of transmission are often unclear. Until further studies clarify transmission modes, airborne and contact precautions, as well as eye protection, should be added to standard precautions to reduce the risk of transmission. 26. Infection prevention and control strategies in healthcare facilities should include early recognition and source control, administrative controls, environmental and engineering controls, and the appropriate use of PPE. 27. Early recognition and source control are critical to reducing the dissemination of infectious agents from infected patients, who are the primary source of pathogens in healthcare settings. 28. Administrative controls require healthcare facility management to ensure the availability of resources for IPC measures, including sustainable IPC infrastructures, clear policies, access to laboratory testing, and appropriate clinical triage and patient placement. 29. Environmental and engineering controls aim to reduce the concentration of infectious respiratory aerosols in the air and minimize surface contamination. Examples include adequate ventilation and spatial separation of at least 1 meter between patients. 30. The appropriate use of PPE further reduces the risk of respiratory pathogen transmission to healthcare workers and others in healthcare facilities. PPE use should be guided by policies and procedures addressing isolation precautions, with effectiveness dependent on adequate supplies, staff training, proper hand hygiene, and appropriate human behavior. 31. All IPC measures should be harmonized to promote a culture of safety within healthcare institutions.
